main.title: MechAssault 2: Lone Wolf
main.subtitle: The pilot can leave the machine
main.summary: MechAssault 2: Lone Wolf is Day 1 Studios and FASA Studio's Xbox action game, released in North America on 28 December 2004. Set in the BattleTech universe, it follows the MechWarrior and allies through a struggle over powerful lost technology. The sequel expands the earlier game's combat by allowing the pilot to leave a BattleMech and use other vehicles. A battlefield can therefore contain several possible ways forward. The machine currently being driven is part of the situation rather than a permanent identity selected before the mission begins.

cards.heading: The pilot can leave the machine
cards.text: MechAssault 2: Lone Wolf is Day 1 Studios and FASA Studio's Xbox action game, released in North America on 28 December 2004. Set in the BattleTech universe, it follows the MechWarrior and allies through a struggle over powerful lost technology. The sequel expands the earlier game's combat by allowing the pilot to leave a BattleMech and use other vehicles. A battlefield can therefore contain several possible ways forward. The machine currently being driven is part of the situation rather than a permanent identity selected before the mission begins.

cards.heading: A smaller suit can take a larger vehicle
cards.text: Tanks, turrets, VTOL aircraft and powered armour offer different ways to engage an encounter. BattleArmor lets the player approach a hostile machine and attempt a neurohack, ejecting its pilot and taking control. Leaving a vehicle creates risk, but it can also supply the means of acquiring a more useful one. The player has to recognise what is nearby and when changing machines is worth the exposure. That movement between scales gives the sequel its central distinction: a comparatively small pilot can redirect the fight by taking possession of its strongest equipment.

cards.heading: An online sequel built around changing roles
cards.text: The developers expanded networking and online features after the original became one of Xbox Live's early showcase games. Multiplayer could draw on the same variety of vehicles and responsibilities seen in the campaign, making the choice of role important to the group. The story's search for data cores connects those battles through an escalating threat within the Inner Sphere. Lone Wolf broadens MechAssault by making the surrounding battlefield more usable. A mech, a tank and a suit of armour become connected options that the player can move between during the action.

main.title: Gran Turismo 4
main.subtitle: Collecting, driving and photographing a world of cars
main.summary: On December 28, 2004, Polyphony Digital released Gran Turismo 4 in Japan for PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: A larger garage for PlayStation 2
cards.text: Gran Turismo 4 is Polyphony Digital's driving simulation for PlayStation 2, first released in Japan on December 28, 2004. More than seven hundred cars from eighty manufacturers compete across over fifty locations. Collecting and modifying vehicles gives the career its progression, while their different weight, power and drivetrains demand changes in driving technique. Two additions offer other ways to enjoy the collection: B-Spec puts the player in charge of a driver, and Photo Mode makes the cars photographic subjects.

cards.heading: Directing the driver in B-Spec
cards.text: B-Spec lets the player direct a computer-controlled driver. Watching the race, they adjust the pace, request overtakes and decide when the situation calls for a more aggressive approach. The car's capabilities still matter, but the player now studies the race from outside the cockpit. A quick driver can be asked to push harder; a difficult situation can call for caution. It gives the collection another use, allowing a race to be approached through instructions and strategy.

cards.heading: Finding a photograph in the garage
cards.text: Photo Mode takes cars to dedicated locations where the player can concentrate on framing an image. Shapes, paintwork and small details that pass quickly during a race become the subject of a still photograph. It offers a reason to return to a favourite model even after its competitive usefulness has faded. The same collection can supply a car for a difficult event or an image that records the player's taste.

cards.heading: Learning the differences between cars
cards.text: The garage places economy cars, sports cars, prototypes and competition machines alongside one another. Progression often asks the player to use vehicles far removed from the fastest supercars. Moving between them makes differences in weight, drivetrain and power easier to feel: a technique learned in one car may need adjusting in another. Over time, a familiar model also recalls the races it helped win and the changes made to its setup. Collecting becomes part of learning how the cars behave.

cards.heading: Reading weight and grip
cards.text: Polyphony pushed the PlayStation 2's physics, graphics and controls while maintaining the response needed for racing. The cars have to communicate changes in grip and weight as they accelerate, brake and turn. A detailed model is useful to the simulation when its behaviour also gives the driver something to read and respond to. With hundreds of vehicles to compare, these differences give the catalogue much of its appeal.

main.title: Xbox 360
main.subtitle: Xbox 360 Puts the Player Profile at the Center of the Console
main.summary: On November 22, 2005, Xbox 360 reaches North American stores, opening a rollout that will reach Europe on December 2 and Japan on December 10.

cards.heading: A console built around the player profile
cards.text: Xbox 360 launched in North America on November 22, 2005, followed by Europe on December 2 and Japan on December 10. Microsoft's console combined high-definition games with an operating system built around a persistent player profile. A Gamertag links friends, achievements and online activity across games, while Xbox Live Marketplace brings downloads into the dashboard. Xbox Live had begun on the first Xbox; its deeper integration into the new console made these services part of everyday use.

cards.heading: The same Gamertag across games
cards.text: The Gamertag gives players an identity that follows them between games and onto Xbox.com. Friends can see one another's presence and status, while the Gamercard collects information to share and compare. Moving to another game preserves those connections. The dashboard gives them a place outside any individual title, making the player's profile an ongoing record of activity across the catalogue.

cards.heading: Keeping an achievement record
cards.text: Achievements record milestones on the Xbox Live profile and award Gamerscore points. A developer can recognise progress through the main game or set an optional challenge that encourages a different way to play. Players can then compare their results with friends and keep that record after moving to another title. Other platforms later introduced trophies and similar systems. On Xbox 360, achievements were part of the profile and dashboard from launch.

cards.heading: Downloading from the dashboard
cards.text: Xbox Live Marketplace launched with more than four hundred items, including demos, trailers, themes, gamer pictures and premium content. A player could discover a game and download its demo directly through the console. Microsoft Points supplied the currency for purchases, adding a conversion between money and the displayed price. Downloads and later additions gave the dashboard a continuing role in how players found and used their games.

cards.heading: Eighteen games at the North American launch
cards.text: Eighteen games accompanied the North American launch. Kameo, Perfect Dark Zero and Project Gotham Racing 3 sat alongside titles from other publishers, including Call of Duty 2 and Need for Speed: Most Wanted. The range offered racing, sports, shooters and other reasons to try the new hardware. High-definition presentation and online features appeared across the line-up, giving early owners several ways to experience the console from its first day.

main.title: Guitar Hero guitar controller
main.subtitle: A plastic guitar makes rhythm physical
main.summary: Guitar Hero brought its guitar-shaped controller to PlayStation 2 in 2005.

cards.heading: Frets without strings
cards.text: Guitar Hero began on PlayStation 2 in 2005. Its guitar-shaped controller replaced strings with coloured fret buttons and a strum bar. Players held the indicated buttons and strummed as notes reached the target on screen. The shape made the familiar rhythm-game task feel like a small stage performance.

cards.heading: A controller for a particular kind of play
cards.text: Compatible Guitar Hero software supplies the songs and judges the player's timing, while the controller turns each incoming note into a combination of fret buttons and strums. Later releases introduced different guitar designs and platform connections. Choosing an accessory therefore means checking which game and console it supports.

main.title: Kameo: Elements of Power
main.subtitle: A family rescue
main.summary: Kameo: Elements of Power is Rare's 2005 action adventure for Xbox 360. Kameo sets out to rescue her family from the troll king Thorn, drawing on the powers of elemental warriors. Changing form gives her different ways to fight and move, carrying the journey between lively landscapes and larger confrontations.

cards.heading: A family rescue
cards.text: Kameo: Elements of Power is Rare's 2005 action adventure for Xbox 360. Kameo sets out to rescue her family from the troll king Thorn, drawing on the powers of elemental warriors. Changing form gives her different ways to fight and move, carrying the journey between lively landscapes and larger confrontations.

cards.heading: Choosing a form
cards.text: The elemental powers cover plant, water, rock, ice and fire. Choosing a form changes the next action available, so recognising the immediate problem is part of preparing to meet it. An attack suited to one enemy can be less helpful when the surroundings demand another approach. The useful response comes from the collection of forms Kameo has learned to use.

cards.heading: Learning the landscape
cards.text: Exploration gives those changes a purpose beyond the next group of trolls. A new ability can make another part of a place accessible, encouraging a return with a different form ready. The player learns the landscape and the warriors together. Recognising where a power belongs becomes another way of remembering a route through the adventure.

cards.heading: Changing the response
cards.text: Combat asks the player to move between abilities while enemies keep approaching. A strong opening can be followed with another form, making a useful sequence out of actions that would be less effective alone. Rare's colourful characters keep each transformation easy to recognise. The changing body makes the player's current choice visible inside the encounter, alongside the enemies it must deal with.

main.title: Mario Kart DS
main.summary: Mario Kart DS is a 2005 kart racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: Mario Kart DS brought Nintendo's kart racing series to Nintendo DS in 2005. Mario characters race on courses drawn from their world, using items to compete for position. It was the fifth main entry, the second made for a handheld, and the first to offer racing through Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection. Released in November in North America, Europe and Australia and in December in Japan, it combined portable play with a new way to race online.

Reviewers praised the handling, single-player content and multiplayer options, particularly online racing. Criticism included the limits of that mode and the computer opponents' ability to catch up. Awards from GameSpot, IGN and G-Phoria accompanied its commercial success. With 23.6 million copies sold worldwide in the figures reported by March 2016, it stood among the largest successes on Nintendo DS. The game later returned through Wii U's Virtual Console.

main.title: Psychonauts
main.summary: Psychonauts is a 2005 platform game developed by Double Fine Productions and published by Majesco for Microsoft Windows, Xbox, and PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: A mind becomes a place to explore
cards.text: Psychonauts is a 2005 platform game developed by Double Fine Productions and published by Majesco for Microsoft Windows, Xbox, and PlayStation 2. The game follows Razputin "Raz" Aquato, a young boy gifted with psychic abilities, who runs away from a circus to try to sneak into a summer camp for those with similar powers to become a "Psychonaut", a spy with psychic abilities. He finds that there is a sinister plot occurring at the camp that only he can stop. The game is centered on exploring the strange and imaginative minds of various characters that Raz encounters as a Psychonaut-in-training/"Psycadet" to help them overcome their fears or memories of their past, so as to gain their help and progress in the game. Raz gains use of several psychic abilities during the game that are used for both attacking foes and solving puzzles.

cards.heading: An idea survives a change of publisher
cards.text: Psychonauts was based on an abandoned concept that Double Fine founder Tim Schafer had during his previous development of Full Throttle. The game was initially backed by Microsoft's Ed Fries as a premiere title for the original Xbox console, but several internal and external issues led to difficulties for Double Fine in meeting various milestones and responding to testing feedback. Following Fries' departure in 2004, Microsoft dropped the publishing rights, making the game's future unclear. Double Fine was able to secure Majesco as a publisher a few months later allowing them to complete the game after four and a half years of development.

cards.heading: A cult following and a digital second life
cards.text: Psychonauts won industry awards and developed a cult following, although publisher Majesco suffered serious financial losses after its release. In 2011, Double Fine acquired the rights and republished the game digitally, updating it for modern systems and bringing it to Mac and Linux. The studio reported that these later sales exceeded those of the original release, with cumulative sales approaching 1.7 million by December 2015. The following years brought a sequel: Psychonauts 2 was announced that month and released on August 25,2021.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap
main.subtitle: A Vast Kingdom Seen From a Few Centimeters
main.summary: On January 10, 2005 The Minish Cap reaches North America after its 2004 debut in Japan and Europe.

cards.heading: An adventure at two scales
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap is Capcom and Nintendo's Game Boy Advance adventure built around Link's ability to become tiny. Puddles, furniture and small openings change their significance when he shrinks to the size of the Minish. Its compact Hyrule combines dungeons, tools and reasons to return to familiar locations. Following its 2004 debut in Japan and Europe, the game reached North America on January 10, 2005.

cards.heading: Finding a route as a Minish
cards.text: At specific points, Link uses the cap Ezlo to shrink. An ordinary step can become a wall and a tiny opening can offer a new route. The transformation lets a location be explored at two different scales. Returning to a familiar area can therefore reveal something the player could previously see but could not reach. Small details give the Game Boy Advance maps much of their variety.

cards.heading: Matching Kinstone fragments
cards.text: Kinstones come in fragments that Link can match with pieces held by characters across Hyrule. A successful fusion can reveal a chest, open a passage or change something elsewhere. Collecting pieces gives the player a reason to speak to people and revisit places. A useful encounter may pay off in another part of the world, connecting the smaller discoveries made during the journey.

cards.heading: Flagship and Nintendo build a handheld Zelda
cards.text: Flagship, the Capcom-affiliated studio that worked on the Oracle games, collaborated with Nintendo on The Minish Cap. Director Hidemaro Fujibayashi described the challenge of proposing new ideas within Zelda's familiar pattern of dungeons, tools and exploration. Its pixel art carries some of The Wind Waker's liveliness into a handheld setting. Fujibayashi later continued working on Zelda at Nintendo.

main.title: Resident Evil 4
main.subtitle: Fear Moves Behind the Camera
main.summary: On January 11, 2005 Resident Evil 4 is released in North America on GameCube and shifts the balance of the entire series.

cards.heading: Leon faces a different kind of horror
cards.text: Resident Evil 4 follows Leon through a horror adventure built around close aiming and aggressive groups of enemies. Capcom replaced the series' familiar fixed views with a camera near his shoulder, changing how players judge the space ahead and respond to danger. Limited ammunition and the need to manage threats remain central. First released in North America for GameCube on January 11, 2005, the game became an influential model for third-person action.

cards.heading: Reconsidering the series' conventions
cards.text: Capcom's postmortem describes a deliberate reconsideration of the series' conventions, including how it produced fear. Resident Evil 4 retains ammunition shortages, monsters and tension while changing the pace of an encounter. The player aims at approaching enemies, repositions and tries to keep a group under control. This new approach gave the developers ways to surprise an audience already familiar with the earlier games.

cards.heading: A camera close behind the shoulder
cards.text: The camera sits close behind Leon, keeping his body in view while allowing precise aim. Watching a target also limits the player's awareness of what is happening beyond that view. Looking, shooting and finding a useful position all take attention. Shinji Mikami later recalled that he had not expected the camera to become so influential. Its combination of proximity and visible aiming became a reference point for later third-person games.

cards.heading: Making the crowd work on GameCube
cards.text: Ganados approach in groups, move around obstacles and threaten to close the player's escape routes. The crowd also made demands on the hardware. Capcom described scenes with as many as twenty-five characters and several versions of Ganado models, using different geometry and textures according to distance and available memory. Those choices let the village fill with opponents while keeping their movements readable enough for the player to respond.

main.title: Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath
main.summary: Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath is an action-adventure video game developed by Oddworld Inhabitants and published by Electronic Arts for the Xbox.

cards.text: Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath is an action-adventure video game developed by Oddworld Inhabitants and published by Electronic Arts for the Xbox. It was released on January 25, 2005, and is the fourth overall entry of the Oddworld series.

The game details the adventures of Stranger, a fearsome bounty hunter. Throughout the game, Stranger pursues and captures outlaws in order to collect bounties. The goal is to ultimately earn enough moolah (in-game money) to pay for a mysterious life-saving operation. One of the most notable features is the "live ammunition" system, which is ammunition made of living creatures like fictional insects and small mammals, each with different uses and effects against enemies.

The game was released on Steam in December 2010 as part of the Oddboxx, a collection which includes all the Oddworld games. A version for the PlayStation 3 was released via the PlayStation Network in December 2011. A mobile build was released in 2014 for Android and iOS. An Ouya build was released in January 2015. A Nintendo Switch port was released in January 2020, co-published by Microids. The game was released on Xbox One and PlayStation 4 (later made playable on PlayStation 5) on February 11, 2022.
